tracks.transcriptSource: Look up on a clear day, and the sky is blue. But sunlight itself is white. So where does the blue come from?

tracks.timingEvidence: WAV header duration plus ffprobe; per-sentence synthesis
tracks.transcriptSource: The answer is written in the air itself. Tiny molecules of nitrogen and oxygen, far smaller than a wave of light.

tracks.timingEvidence: WAV header duration plus ffprobe; per-sentence synthesis
tracks.transcriptSource: When sunlight hits them, they scatter short blue wavelengths in every direction, several times more strongly than red.

tracks.timingEvidence: WAV header duration plus ffprobe; per-sentence synthesis
tracks.transcriptSource: That scattered blue light reaches your eyes from everywhere overhead. That is why the whole sky glows blue.

tracks.timingEvidence: WAV header duration plus ffprobe; per-sentence synthesis
tracks.transcriptSource: Violet is scattered even more, but there is less of it in sunlight, and your eyes are less sensitive to it.

tracks.timingEvidence: WAV header duration plus ffprobe; per-sentence synthesis
tracks.transcriptSource: At sunset, sunlight crosses much more air. The blue is scattered away, and the reds and oranges remain.

tracks.timingEvidence: WAV header duration plus ffprobe; per-sentence synthesis
tracks.transcriptSource: Dust and pollution scatter all colors equally, which is why a hazy sky looks pale and white.

tracks.timingEvidence: WAV header duration plus ffprobe; per-sentence synthesis
tracks.transcriptSource: So the blue sky is not a thing. It is sunlight, rearranged by the air. Thanks for watching.
